beats.trigger: ## Security
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: You can't tell if your agent is safe from its output.
beats.got: Reading what an agent says doesn't show whether it's safe, so you need a separate check.

beats.trigger: Prework covers personal skills and agent risk layered on normal security.
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: **Evaluate** residual risk: what is left, and what future sessions need before touching the system
beats.got: A list of verbs. I could have read it in the 2017 deck.

beats.trigger: Name what you'd want to check before letting this near a real stakeholder.
beats.got: I'm asked to name my own worries first. That's fair.

beats.trigger: A tool call is text crossing a boundary into action.
beats.got: The agent writes text and a harness turns it into actions. That's a clear way to see where the risk sits.

beats.trigger: Agent systems do not offer certainty.
beats.got: They admit up front that nobody can promise this is safe. I didn't expect that.

beats.trigger: same input, same output.
beats.got: Old security worked because software behaved the same way every time.

beats.trigger: The dangerous move is getting your agent to *decide* to do something harmful with access it has, through well-formed English in a document it reads.
beats.got: A plain document can attack the agent, so the attack surface is the text it reads. That is new and I can see why it matters.

beats.trigger: Scope (give the agent less). Split (two agents, different trust levels). Filter (post-process output). Gate (human approves). Review (a second agent judges).
beats.got: Five mitigations. It's a sensible list, close to normal risk work.

beats.trigger: **"I can't tell"** is a real answer.
beats.got: You're allowed to say you don't know, and you write down what's left. I like that.

beats.trigger: Scope it down far enough and the system is safe and useless.
beats.got: Safety and usefulness trade off, and someone has to sign for the balance.

beats.trigger: Expect it to cost you a feature.
beats.got: The best mitigation is not connecting something, and that costs capability. They say so plainly.

beats.trigger: Damn, this is complex stuff.
beats.got: The honest bit is good. The 'discipline carries' line is a little preachy.

beats.trigger: a skill is a reusable check you run again instead of re-prompting from memory.
beats.got: A skill is a saved procedure the agent can run again. Fine, it's a checklist.

beats.trigger: they show which rules files can check and which need judgment, context, or a standing evidence check.
beats.got: The agent ran our policy files against the system and sorted rules into checkable and needs-judgment. I could verify that myself, which is a first.

beats.trigger: Push back on anything that sounds like a generic GDPR brochure.
beats.got: I tell it what actually matters to us and it adjusts. Reasonable.

beats.trigger: Expect many questions; the agent keeps probing both lenses over several rounds.
beats.got: Forty minutes of Q&A to produce one checklist file.

beats.trigger: "You choose. Optimise for what I can't steer."
beats.got: When the questions run out of my knowledge I hand the decision back. That's practical.

beats.trigger: Run `ls .claude/skills/agent-audit/` to confirm.
beats.got: Admin: save the file and check it's there.

beats.trigger: Agent mitigations sit on top of normal company controls, not in place of them.
beats.got: This doesn't replace our existing security. Good, someone would have asked.

beats.trigger: The goal is the loop (assess, mitigate, reassess residual), not a clean bill of health.
beats.got: They aren't promising a pass. It's an audit that finds things.

beats.trigger: Type `/` and look for `/agent-audit` in the autocomplete list.
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: Expect the reusable check to find things you did not think about, and to leave things "I can't tell" you thought were settled.
beats.got: The audit turned up things we hadn't considered and showed that some rules we thought were settled aren't. I can test that against our own files.

beats.trigger: The uncomfortable feeling is the evidence.
beats.got: A ranked list of how my agent could be misled or leak. Unsettling, and probably useful.

beats.trigger: The risk remains. That is expected. Name it, accept it on record, and stop there.
beats.got: You fix one thing, the risk is smaller but still there, and you write that down. No pretence it's solved.

beats.trigger: The narrow question the expert can answer is sitting in the report.
beats.got: When the agent can't settle something, take a narrow question to legal or security. Sensible.

beats.trigger: Risk control, done for every risk you found, separates a prototype from a production agent.
beats.got: We did one risk. A real agent needs all of them done, and that's the real work.

beats.trigger: The reusable check is the expert in the room, and it carries to the next agent.
beats.got: A recap. 'Expert in the room' oversells a checklist a bit.

beats.trigger: The unease stays.
beats.got: The agent writes lessons into the instructions file for next time.

beats.trigger: A skill is not a deployed service and does not settle ownership.
beats.got: You can package other recurring checks as skills too.

beats.trigger: Well-formed English is the attack surface, even via sources.
beats.got: The summary matches what I took away.

beats.trigger: Without the two sentences, you'll be writing them while the rest of the room is already comparing detectors.
beats.got: Homework, with a mild nudge.

beats.trigger: What check was missing around the agent's output?
beats.got: Two real cases of an organisation missing a check on AI output. Cases beat claims, so I'd read them.

take_homes: The risk with agents is the text they read, because a plain document can talk one into doing harm. That is different from the old software story.
You can't prove an agent is safe. You run a check, fix one thing, write down what's left and who accepted it.
The cheapest fix is not connecting something, and it costs a feature.

monday.move: Run the policy files against one agent we already have and read the 'I can't tell' rows. Nothing more.
monday.who: me, then maybe our security lead
monday.when: if a quiet hour turns up this week
monday.stop_condition: The report is vague or generic, or I'd need to be convinced it's worth the time.

misconception.why: The attack surface here is new, and it doesn't wait for me to decide. Wait-and-see is still a fair guess about hype but a poor one about exposure. I'm not converted.

one_line: First training in a while that said out loud it can't promise anything. The audit part you can test yourself, which beats the usual slides.
